title: Why Do Nuclear Plants Have Those Giant Towers?
description:
When people picture a nuclear power plant, they picture giant curved towers with white clouds pouring out of them. Most people think those clouds are smoke, or even radiation. They are neither. They are water vapor, the same stuff as a cloud in the sky. And the towers are not even the nuclear part. Today, eleven parts of a nuclear power plant, and why each one exists, starting with those towers.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 11 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:11 1. The curved tower
2:21 2. The waist of the tower
3:27 3. The plant without towers
4:37 4. The concrete dome
5:51 5. The rods that stop the reaction
7:02 6. The pellet the size of a fingertip
8:08 7. The pool of glowing blue water
9:16 8. The thick steel pot
10:27 9. The control room
11:41 10. The emergency generators
12:54 11. The cloud on the horizon
13:59 The verdict

Sources:
- Natural draft cooling towers (hyperboloid shape, thin shells, evaporation, plumes are water vapour): Wikipedia, "Cooling tower" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooling_tower ; Wikipedia, "Hyperboloid structure" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperboloid_structure ; US NRC, "Cooling towers" glossary https://www.nrc.gov/
- Once-through cooling, heat waves and output reductions: Wikipedia, "Nuclear power plant" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power_plant ; EDF / French nuclear operator notices
- Jellyfish shutdowns (Torness 2011, Oskarshamn 2013): BBC News reports
- Containment buildings: US NRC, "Containment structure" https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/basic-ref/glossary/containment-structure.html
- Three Mile Island (28 March 1979; stuck-open PORV, misleading indicator, control room and simulator reforms): Kemeny Commission Report (1979) ; US NRC Backgrounder https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/doc-collections/fact-sheets/3mile-isle.html
- Chernobyl (1986, no Western-style containment): Wikipedia, "Chernobyl disaster" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chernobyl_disaster
- Control rods, scram and decay heat: US NRC glossary ; Wikipedia, "Control rod" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_rod ; Wikipedia, "Decay heat" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decay_heat
- Fuel pellets (one pellet ~ one ton of coal): Nuclear Energy Institute https://www.nei.org/ ; US DOE, "Nuclear Fuel Facts"
- Cherenkov radiation and spent fuel pools, dry casks: Wikipedia, "Cherenkov radiation" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherenkov_radiation ; US NRC, "Spent Fuel Storage" https://www.nrc.gov/waste/spent-fuel-storage.html
- PWR pressure vessel (~155 bar, ~300 °C), surveillance capsules: Wikipedia, "Pressurized water reactor" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressurized_water_reactor
- Fukushima Daiichi (11 March 2011, flooded diesel generators, three meltdowns): IAEA, "The Fukushima Daiichi Accident" (2015) https://www.iaea.org/
